posts.title: Design Agency Onboarding: What Happens First
posts.excerpt: What actually happens after you sign with a design agency — kickoff, discovery, first deliverables, and the feedback loop that follows.
takeaways: Onboarding typically follows four stages: kickoff, access and asset collection, discovery, and first deliverables.
Preparing brand assets, access credentials, and stakeholder availability before kickoff shortens the discovery phase.
Fast, consolidated feedback from one clear approver keeps a project moving; slow or scattered feedback is the most common cause of delay.
Stating priorities before reviewing work gives the agency something concrete to design against, rather than guesswork.

toc.label: What happens after you sign with a design agency?
What should a client prepare before kickoff?
How does communication typically work during onboarding?
What does good client participation look like?
Common onboarding mistakes to avoid
Onboarding readiness checklist
The takeaway

body.html: Once a contract is signed, most design agency onboarding follows a similar shape: a kickoff call to align on goals, a short window to collect brand assets and account access, a discovery phase where the agency researches the audience and competitors, and then a first round of deliverables that opens the ongoing feedback loop. The exact pacing shifts with project size and scope, but that four-part sequence — kickoff, access, discovery, first deliverables — is the backbone of almost every engagement, whether the project is a brand refresh, a new website, or a full product redesign.

Knowing what to expect in those opening weeks matters more than it seems. A client who understands the shape of onboarding can prepare the right materials ahead of time, answer questions faster, and avoid the stop-start pattern that stretches timelines and frustrates both sides. It also sets expectations correctly: the first few weeks of a project are rarely about seeing polished screens — they are about making sure the work that follows is pointed in the right direction. Clients who expect visuals immediately sometimes read a quiet discovery phase as a lack of progress, when in most cases it is the opposite.

This guide walks through what actually happens after you sign with a design agency, what to have ready before the first call, how communication tends to work, and the habits that separate projects that move quickly from ones that stall.
What happens after you sign with a design agency?

The period right after signing is less about design work and more about setup. Agencies use this time to gather context, confirm scope, and build the foundation the actual design and development work will sit on. Skipping or rushing this stage is one of the more common reasons projects lose momentum later, because decisions made without enough context tend to get revisited.
The kickoff call

This is usually the first real conversation after the contract is signed. The agency and client team walk through goals, audience, scope, and the rough shape of the timeline together. It is also where everyone meets the people they will be working with for the next several weeks or months, which matters more than it sounds — a kickoff call with the right stakeholders in the room tends to surface misalignments early, before they turn into rework. A good kickoff usually ends with a shared understanding of what "done" looks like for the first phase, not just a list of deliverables and dates.
Access and asset collection

Immediately after kickoff, the agency will ask for brand files, existing research, analytics access, and any logins needed to audit the current site, product, or systems. This step is often the quiet bottleneck of onboarding — not because the work is hard, but because gathering scattered credentials and files across a team takes longer than anyone expects. Clients who have this ready at signing routinely move through the first two weeks faster than those who collect it piecemeal, chasing down a password here and a font file there while the agency waits to start.
The discovery phase

With access in hand, the agency researches the audience, reviews competitors, and audits what already exists — the current site, the current brand, or the current product, depending on scope. Discovery is where most of the thinking happens before any visual work begins: identifying what is working, what isn't, where competitors are strong or weak, and what the audience actually needs from the end result. Projects that skip or shorten discovery tend to produce designs that look fine in isolation but miss something the client only notices once it is in front of them, which usually means a slower first review round, not a faster one. It is also common for discovery to surface questions the client hadn't considered — about priorities, audience segments, or technical constraints — which is part of why this phase rarely moves as fast as a kickoff call alone might suggest.
Early deliverables and the first feedback loop

The first concepts, wireframes, or direction options usually arrive once discovery findings are in place. This is the point where the relationship shifts from information-gathering to collaboration — the client reviews, the agency explains the reasoning behind choices, and feedback starts shaping the next round. How this first loop goes often sets the tone for the rest of the project, which is part of why clear, consolidated feedback matters so much in these early rounds. A first round that goes well usually isn't the one with zero feedback — it's the one where the feedback is specific, tied to the project's goals, and gathered from the right people before it reaches the agency.
What should a client prepare before kickoff?

Preparation before the first call is one of the clearest levers a client has over how smoothly onboarding goes. None of it requires special expertise — it is mostly a matter of gathering what already exists and deciding who needs to be in the room.

items: Brand assets — logo files, fonts, brand guidelines, and any existing style references, even informal ones.
Access and credentials — CMS, hosting, domain, and analytics logins so the agency can audit what is already in place.
Stakeholder availability — a named point of contact and a short list of who needs to approve major decisions.
Examples the client likes — sites, products, or competitors worth referencing, plus anything they want to avoid.

body.html: If a client is still deciding which agency to work with at all, it is worth reading through how to choose a web design agency and the list of questions to ask a design agency before signing — the answers to those questions often reveal how structured an agency's onboarding process actually is.

rows: Project lead on both sides, key stakeholders
Research findings, audience and competitor notes
Reactions to initial concepts or wireframes

body.html: A useful companion to this preparation is a written brief. Agencies that ask for one early are usually trying to avoid guesswork later — see what belongs in a website design brief for a sense of what that document should include before the first call even happens.
How does communication typically work during onboarding?

Communication patterns vary by agency, but a few habits show up often enough to call common rather than universal. Many teams default to async updates — short written check-ins between calls — rather than daily meetings, since onboarding work (research, asset organization, early concepts) does not always need a live conversation to move forward. Review cadence tends to follow the shape of the deliverables rather than the calendar: a call or written summary after discovery wraps, another after the first concepts are ready, rather than a fixed weekly rhythm regardless of what is actually done.

This is a pattern, not a rule. Smaller projects sometimes run on tighter, more frequent check-ins; larger ones with more stakeholders often need more structure and more advance notice before reviews. What tends to matter more than the exact cadence is clarity about where things stand and what is coming next, so neither side is guessing.
Tools and documentation

Most agencies run onboarding through a mix of a shared project board, a messaging channel for quick questions, and a shared drive for files and references. None of these tools are unique to design work — they are the same kind of setup most client-facing teams use — but having one agreed place for files and one agreed place for conversation cuts down on the back-and-forth of "did you see the note I sent" that otherwise eats into review time. A short written summary after each major call, even an informal one, also tends to prevent the same question from being asked twice a few weeks later.
What does good client participation look like?

Participation is where a lot of onboarding timelines are actually won or lost. The work itself — research, design, iteration — takes roughly the time it takes. What varies wildly between projects is how long feedback takes to come back, how many people weigh in, and how clear the priorities are when it does.
What slows a project down

A few habits reliably add weeks to a timeline. Feedback that sits untouched for two or three weeks loses momentum and forces the team to re-familiarize itself with the work before responding to notes. Having many stakeholders review separately, rather than consolidating into one note, often produces conflicting direction that is harder to resolve than if no feedback had come in at all — one reviewer asking for bolder colors while another asks for something more subdued leaves the agency with no clear direction to design toward. And reviewing work without stating what matters most — tone, functionality, speed to launch — leaves the agency guessing at priorities instead of designing against them.

None of this is about clients being difficult. In most cases, slow feedback and scattered approvals come from genuine scheduling pressure, not a lack of interest in the project. The fix is rarely about trying harder — it's about agreeing on a feedback process at kickoff, so turnaround time and approval order are expectations from the start rather than something negotiated mid-project when a deadline is already at risk.

rows: Context is lost on both sides, momentum stalls
Conflicting notes create extra rework cycles
Feedback becomes subjective instead of goal-driven
Timeline and budget assumptions no longer hold

body.html: Common onboarding mistakes to avoid

items: Slow feedback turnaround. Even a short delay compounds across multiple review rounds — agreeing on a feedback window up front helps both sides plan around it.
Too many stakeholders approving at once. One named decision-maker per phase, gathering input beforehand, tends to move faster than open review by committee.
Unclear priorities. Feedback like "make it pop" is hard to act on; feedback tied to a goal — conversions, clarity, brand tone — is not.
Incomplete access at kickoff. Partial logins or missing assets turn discovery into a back-and-forth instead of a focused research phase.
Scope conversations held too late. Raising a new requirement mid-project causes far more rework than flagging it during kickoff, even informally.

body.html: Agencies that scope work by project rather than ongoing retainer tend to be more sensitive to these mistakes, since added scope has a more direct effect on budget and timeline. The difference matters enough that it is worth understanding before signing — see retainer vs. project-based agency pricing for how that choice can shape how flexible onboarding and later scope changes will feel.
Onboarding readiness checklist
Before the first call, a client is in good shape if they can check off most of the following:

items: Brand assets and any existing guidelines are gathered in one place.
Access credentials for the CMS, hosting, domain, and analytics are ready to share.
A single point of contact is named for day-to-day questions.
The stakeholders who need to approve major decisions are identified in advance.
A short list of reference sites or products — liked and disliked — is ready to discuss.
Internal availability for a kickoff call and a first feedback round is confirmed.
Top priorities for the project are written down, even informally, before the first review.

body.html: None of this needs to be polished. A messy folder of logos and a half-finished list of competitor sites is still far more useful than starting from nothing — the goal is to save the first weeks for research and direction, not for chasing down files.
The takeaway

Design agency onboarding is not a black box — it tends to follow a kickoff call, an access and asset handoff, a discovery phase, and a first round of deliverables that opens the feedback loop. What a client controls most is preparation and participation: having assets and access ready, naming one clear approver, stating priorities up front, and turning feedback around consolidated and on time. Projects that get these right tend to move through the early weeks with far less friction than those that don't. If it would help to talk through what onboarding would look like for a specific project, get in touch with our team.

faq.q: What is the first step in design agency onboarding?
faq.a: The first step is usually a kickoff call, where the agency and client team align on goals, scope, and the rough timeline before any research or design work begins.

faq.q: How long does agency onboarding usually take?
faq.a: There's no universal number, but discovery and the first round of deliverables commonly take a few weeks depending on project scope — the client's preparation and feedback speed affect this more than the agency's internal process.

faq.q: What should a client have ready before the first call?
faq.a: Brand assets, access credentials for relevant platforms, a named point of contact, and a short list of stakeholders who need to approve decisions.

faq.q: Why does feedback turnaround matter so much during onboarding?
faq.a: Because early feedback loops set the pace for the rest of the project — slow or inconsistent feedback in the first rounds tends to compound into longer delays later on.

faq.q: Should one person or multiple stakeholders approve each phase?
faq.a: One named approver per phase, who gathers input beforehand, is far more common and leads to fewer conflicting revisions than open review by several people at once.

posts.title: Core Web Vitals Explained: A Practical Guide for 2026
posts.excerpt: What LCP, INP, and CLS mean for SEO and AI search, and how design and dev teams improve each score in practice.
takeaways: Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) are part of Google's ranking signal and increasingly shape whether AI search tools can crawl and cite a page.

LCP is improved mainly through image optimization, font loading, and hosting/CDN choices; INP through script discipline and shorter main-thread tasks; CLS through reserved space for images, embeds, and fonts.
Check field data (Search Console, CrUX) and lab data (PageSpeed Insights, Lighthouse) together, since they answer different questions.
Quick fixes (images, fonts, scripts) handle most single-page issues; template-wide or hosting-level problems need a deeper fix.

Why do Core Web Vitals affect SEO and AI search rankings?

The takeaway

body.html: Core Web Vitals are three measurable signals, Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), that Google uses to judge how a page feels to use. They affect traditional search rankings as part of the page experience signal, and they increasingly shape how AI search tools and answer engines decide which pages are reliable enough to cite. The short version: if your pages load slowly, respond sluggishly to taps and clicks, or jump around while loading, both classic search and AI-driven search will quietly rank you behind competitors who fixed those problems first.
What are Core Web Vitals, exactly?
Core Web Vitals are a set of three metrics Google publishes as part of its page experience guidelines. Each one measures a different kind of frustration a visitor can run into:

items: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) measures how long it takes the biggest visible element, usually a hero image, a heading, or a banner, to fully render.
INP (Interaction to Next Paint) measures how long the page takes to visibly respond after someone clicks, taps, or types. It replaced an older metric called First Input Delay in 2024.
CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures how much content shifts position unexpectedly while a page loads or while someone is reading it.

body.html: Google scores each metric against public threshold bands: good, needs improvement, and poor. The table below spells out the official bands for each metric.
Why do Core Web Vitals affect SEO and AI search rankings?

Core Web Vitals are part of Google's page experience signal, which sits alongside content relevance, mobile-friendliness, and security when pages are ranked. On its own, a fast page with weak content will not outrank a strong page with slightly slower load times, but between two similar pages, the faster, more stable one tends to win the tie.

What has changed in the last couple of years is how much weight page quality carries in AI-driven search. AI answer engines and AI crawlers need to fetch, render, and parse a page quickly and reliably before they can summarize or cite it. A page that loads slowly, shifts content around, or buries its main text behind heavy third-party scripts is harder for a crawler to process cleanly and more likely to get skipped in favor of a page that renders fast and stays stable. The underlying logic is simple: a crawler with a time or compute budget for each page will favor the page it can render and extract text from without friction, and a stable, fast-loading page gives it less to work around.

In short, Core Web Vitals used to be mostly a ranking nudge. They are now closer to a basic requirement for being read at all by the systems that increasingly decide what shows up in a search result or an AI answer.
How do you improve LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)?
LCP problems almost always trace back to one of three causes: a large unoptimized image, a slow server response, or render-blocking resources that delay the main content from appearing.
Image optimization

The hero image or banner is usually the LCP element on marketing pages. Compress it, serve it in a modern format like WebP or AVIF, and size it to the dimensions it actually renders at rather than shipping a much larger source file and letting the browser scale it down. Preloading the LCP image with a <link rel="preload"> tag also helps, since it tells the browser to fetch that image earlier instead of discovering it late in the page's loading sequence.
Font loading

Web fonts can delay LCP when the browser has to wait for a font file before it can paint visible text. Using font-display: swap, preloading critical font files, and limiting the number of font weights a page loads all reduce this delay.
Hosting and CDN choices

Server response time (often called Time to First Byte) sets a floor under every other LCP optimization. A page cannot paint content it has not received yet. Hosting on a platform with a content delivery network, caching HTML and assets close to the visitor, and avoiding hosting plans that queue requests under load all shrink that floor. This is one of the reasons we are selective about hosting recommendations in our site speed work, since a slow origin server undoes a lot of front-end optimization before it even starts.
Render-blocking resources

Stylesheets and scripts placed in the page head without any loading hints can delay the browser from painting anything at all, including the LCP element. Inlining the small amount of CSS needed for the visible portion of the page, loading the rest asynchronously, and moving non-critical scripts below the main content all reduce the time between a visitor requesting a page and seeing something useful on it.
How do you improve INP (Interaction to Next Paint)?

INP problems come from the main thread being too busy to respond to input right away. The browser has to finish whatever JavaScript is running before it can process a click or a tap, so the usual fix is reducing how much work runs on the main thread, and when it runs.
Third-party script discipline

Analytics tags, chat widgets, ad scripts, and embedded trackers are the most common source of INP problems on marketing sites. Each one adds JavaScript that competes for the same main thread the page needs for its own interactions. Audit what is actually loading on a page, remove scripts that are not earning their keep, and load the rest with async or defer so they do not block rendering or interaction.
Breaking up long tasks

Any JavaScript task that runs for more than 50 milliseconds can delay the next interaction. Splitting large functions into smaller chunks, deferring non-essential work until after the page is interactive, and avoiding heavy work inside scroll or input event handlers all keep the main thread free to respond. On forms and search boxes specifically, debouncing input handlers so they only fire after someone pauses typing, instead of on every keystroke, removes a surprising amount of unnecessary work from the main thread.
How do you fix CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)?

CLS almost always comes down to content appearing without reserved space for it. Common culprits are images and ads without width and height attributes, web fonts that render a visibly different size than their fallback, and content (banners, cookie notices, promotional bars) that gets injected above existing content after the page has already rendered.

items: Always set explicit width and height (or an aspect-ratio) on images, video embeds, and ad slots so the browser reserves space before the asset loads.
Match fallback font metrics to the web font as closely as possible, or use font-display: optional on pages where layout stability matters more than using the exact brand font on first paint.
Reserve space for dynamically injected elements, like cookie banners or promo bars, instead of letting them push content down after the fact.
Avoid inserting new content above existing content unless it is in direct response to a user action, like expanding a menu.

body.html: What mistakes do teams commonly make with Core Web Vitals?
Most of the Core Web Vitals problems we run into during technical SEO reviews are not exotic. They are the same handful of mistakes repeated across different sites and platforms.

rows: Testing only on a fast office connection
Hides real-world LCP and INP problems that show up on average mobile connections
Test with throttled network and CPU conditions, and check field data from real visitors
Adding every marketing or analytics tool available
Each script adds main-thread work, hurting INP even when individually small
Audit scripts quarterly and remove anything not actively used
Shipping uncompressed images from a CMS
Directly inflates LCP by delaying the largest visible element
Compress and resize on upload, and serve modern formats automatically
Skipping width and height on embedded content
Causes layout shift as embeds and ads load in
Set explicit dimensions or aspect-ratio on every embed
Treating Core Web Vitals as a one-time fix
Scores drift as new content, scripts, and campaigns get added
Re-check scores after every major release, not just once a year

body.html: How do you check your Core Web Vitals scores?
There are two kinds of data worth checking, and they answer different questions:

items: Field data comes from real visitors over the past 28 days, via the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX). Google Search Console's Core Web Vitals report and PageSpeed Insights both surface this. It reflects what actual visitors on actual devices and networks experienced, which is also the data search ranking systems use.

Lab data comes from a single simulated test run, through tools like Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights' lab section. It is useful for diagnosing what is slow and why, but it will not always match field data exactly, since it reflects one test condition rather than the spread of real visitors.

body.html: We check both together, not just one. Lab data tells us what to fix; field data tells us whether the fix actually moved the numbers that matter for ranking. If you are auditing a whole site rather than one page, Search Console's report groups pages by URL pattern, which is usually the fastest way to spot a template-wide problem instead of chasing one slow page at a time.
Quick fixes vs. deeper fixes: how do you prioritize?

Not every Core Web Vitals problem deserves the same amount of engineering time. Some fixes take an afternoon; others mean restructuring how a page or a whole site is built. Knowing which category a problem falls into before committing time to it keeps a performance pass from stalling out.

rows: Compressing images, adding width/height attributes, deferring a script, preloading a font
Rebuilding a page template, changing hosting or CDN setup, restructuring how third-party scripts load sitewide

body.html: A practical decision guide we use with clients:

items: If a single page is failing, start with quick fixes on that page's images, fonts, and third-party scripts before touching infrastructure.

If most pages on a template are failing the same metric, the problem is probably in the template or a shared script, not any individual page, and a deeper fix at the template level will pay off faster than fixing pages one by one.

If field data and lab data disagree sharply, suspect device or network variance among real visitors rather than a single broken element, and dig into the field data segments (device type, connection speed) before changing code.
If scores are borderline rather than failing, a quick fix is often enough; if a metric is deep in the poor range, it usually points to a structural issue that quick fixes will only partly address.

body.html: We also treat Core Web Vitals work as a standing part of a site's maintenance, not a one-off project. A page that scores well at launch can drift into the needs-improvement range six months later simply because a new campaign script, a heavier hero video, or an extra tracking pixel got added along the way. Building a quarterly check into a site's regular maintenance, alongside the kind of review we run through our Webflow SEO checklist, catches that drift before it shows up as a ranking problem.
A short checklist before you call a page "fixed"

items: Hero image and any above-the-fold images are compressed, correctly sized, and preloaded if they are the LCP element.
Critical fonts are preloaded and set to swap or optional, with no more than two or three weights loading per page.
Every image, video, and ad slot has explicit dimensions or an aspect-ratio set.
Third-party scripts are audited, deferred, or removed if they are not earning their place.
Field data in Search Console confirms the fix, not just a single lab test run.

body.html: The takeaway

Core Web Vitals are not a one-time technical checkbox. They are an ongoing signal that both classic search rankings and AI search tools use to decide whether a page is worth surfacing, and they drift as new content, scripts, and campaigns get added over time. Start with the metric that is failing hardest, fix the handful of common mistakes above, and recheck field data after every meaningful release. If you would rather have a team that does this work walk through your site's Core Web Vitals with you, we are happy to take a look.

faq.q: What is a good Core Web Vitals score?
faq.a: A page passes when LCP is 2.5 seconds or under, INP is 200 milliseconds or under, and CLS is 0.1 or under, measured from real-visitor field data rather than a single lab test.

faq.q: Do Core Web Vitals really affect Google rankings?
faq.a: Yes, they are part of Google's page experience signal, though content relevance still matters more. Core Web Vitals tend to act as a tiebreaker between otherwise similar pages rather than the deciding factor on their own.

faq.q: Why do Core Web Vitals matter for AI search and AI crawlers?
faq.a: AI crawlers and answer engines need to render and parse a page quickly and reliably before they can summarize or cite it, so slow or unstable pages are more likely to get skipped in favor of fast, stable ones.

faq.q: What is the single biggest Core Web Vitals win for most sites?
faq.a: Compressing and correctly sizing the hero image usually delivers the biggest LCP improvement, since an oversized hero image is the most common cause of a failing LCP score.

faq.q: How often should Core Web Vitals be checked?
faq.a: We recommend checking field data at least quarterly, and again after any major release that adds new scripts, images, or page sections, since scores drift as a site changes.

posts.title: How Long Does MVP Development Really Take To Launch?
posts.excerpt: MVP timelines depend on scope and complexity, not team size. Here are the phases, the real cost drivers, and the mistakes that quietly add delay.
takeaways: MVP timelines are set mainly by scope and complexity, not by team size or budget alone.
Every MVP moves through the same five phases: discovery, design, build, testing, and launch.
Adding user roles, integrations, platforms, or compliance requirements multiplies the work rather than simply adding to it.
A scope that is clearly defined before design starts is the single biggest lever for hitting a realistic launch date.

The takeaway

body.html: How long does MVP development actually take?

There is no single number that answers this well for every project, because "MVP" describes a stage of a product, not a size. A narrowly scoped app with one core user flow and no outside integrations can move through design and build in a tightly managed span of weeks. A multi-role SaaS product with permissions, several integrations, and a compliance review stretches into months before it is ready for real users. What decides which end of that range you land on is not effort or budget alone. It is how clearly the scope is defined before anyone opens a design file, how many outside systems the product depends on, and how fast your team can turn feedback into the next version.

This guide walks through the phases every MVP moves through, the factors that actually stretch or compress a timeline, the mistakes that quietly add time nobody budgeted for, and a short decision guide you can use to check your own launch date against reality.
The short answer

An MVP timeline is set less by the idea and more by the scope behind it. A single-platform product with one clear user flow and no third-party dependencies typically moves from kickoff to launch in a matter of weeks. Add user roles, integrations, a second platform, or a compliance requirement, and the same label, MVP, can take several months, because each addition multiplies the number of screens, states, and edge cases that have to be designed, built, and tested before launch. The fastest path to a realistic date is a scope that has been written down and agreed on before design work starts, not a faster design or development team.
The 5 phases of MVP development (where the time actually goes)

Every MVP, regardless of complexity, moves through the same five phases. Knowing what happens in each one is the easiest way to spot where your own project's timeline is likely to stretch, and which delays are normal versus which ones are a sign something upstream was left unresolved.
Discovery and scoping

This phase sets the ceiling for everything that follows. The goal is a written brief that names the core problem, the must-have features, and what gets cut from version one. A vague brief here tends to resurface as a scope argument during build, which is far more expensive to resolve mid-project than it would have been to settle upfront. Teams that move fastest overall are rarely the ones with the most resources. They are the ones who answered the hard scope questions before design started.
UX and UI design

Design turns the brief into wireframes, a clickable prototype, and the visual system for the core flow. This phase moves fastest when stakeholders review together instead of in separate, staggered rounds that each produce their own set of notes. A tested prototype also catches structural problems while they still cost a redesign, not a rebuild. If your product needs a reusable set of components rather than one-off screens, this is also where a design system gets its foundation, which pays off well beyond the first release.
Build and integration

Engineering turns the design into working software: the core flow, the data model, and any third-party services the product depends on. This is usually the longest phase, and the most sensitive to scope creep, because every state a designer sketched now has to actually work, including the edge cases nobody thought about until they showed up in a pull request. Integrations deserve special attention here, since a dependency on an external API or service ties part of your timeline to another company's release schedule, not just your own.
QA and testing

This phase covers functional testing, fixing edge cases, and a round of testing with real users on the core flow before launch. It looks skippable on a schedule because it produces no new features. Skipping it does not remove the work, though. It just moves the same problems to after launch, where they cost more to fix and are visible to the people you are trying to win over.
Launch and handoff

The final phase covers deploying to production, setting up monitoring, and documenting the system well enough that the team can keep shipping after launch day without re-learning decisions that were only ever in someone's head. A rushed handoff here is a common, quiet source of slowdowns in the weeks right after an MVP ships, since the team is now debugging a live product without the context that got it there.
Why complexity changes the timeline more than anything else

Two products can both be described as an MVP and need very different amounts of work. The difference almost always comes down to complexity: how many user types the product serves, how many systems it depends on, and how much of the experience has to work correctly the first time a real user touches it.

A single-platform product with one audience and no logged-in roles is the easiest case to scope accurately, because there is only one path through the product to design, build, and test. Add a second role, an admin alongside an end user, for example, and the work does not simply double. It multiplies, because every screen now needs to account for what each role can see and do, and every permission boundary needs its own test case. A two-sided marketplace is harder still, because neither side of the product can be properly tested until the other side exists in a usable form. And any MVP that touches payments, health information, or another regulated area inherits review cycles that live outside your team's control, which is often the single hardest part of a timeline to predict with any confidence. Our guide to SaaS MVP development goes deeper into what a multi-role build actually involves.

Before you ask how long a build will take, it is worth writing down which of these complexity tiers your product actually sits in. A rough idea that is secretly a two-sided marketplace with payments attached will never fit a single-platform timeline, no matter how experienced the team you hire is.

rows: Can you describe the core flow in two sentences?
A clear yes usually means the scope is tight enough to move quickly.
Does the product need more than one user role at launch?
Each added role adds real design and testing time, not just a setting to flip.
Does it depend on a system your team does not control?
That dependency's pace becomes part of your timeline, not just your team's.
Does anyone outside the team need to approve or review it?
Budget time for cycles your team cannot shorten just by working harder.

body.html: What actually moves your launch date
Beyond the phase and the complexity tier, a handful of factors decide whether a specific MVP comes in faster or slower than a typical project at the same complexity level.

Scope clarity at kickoff has the biggest effect of any single factor, because every hour spent debating what is in scope during build is an hour the team is not shipping. Integrations come next on the list: every third-party service adds a dependency you do not fully control, from access and documentation gaps to the other company's own release schedule. Targeting more than one platform at once adds real work rather than doubling it cleanly, since shared components still need platform-specific testing and polish. The speed of feedback cycles compounds across every phase that follows it, too. A team that gets same-day answers moves through design and build noticeably faster than one waiting several days for sign-off on each round. Design maturity entering build matters as well: a flow that was tested as a prototype rarely needs the expensive kind of rework that an untested one does once it is already built. Compliance or security review is usually the smallest of these factors day to day, but it can block a launch entirely regardless of how fast everything else moved.
SaaS MVP or single app: does the platform change the math?

A SaaS product and a single consumer app can both be MVPs, but they rarely move at the same pace. A SaaS MVP typically introduces accounts, roles, and a dashboard before a single feature even ships, because the product has to support ongoing use by returning customers, not just a first visit. That groundwork takes real time, but it also tends to pay off, since later features build on an architecture that already understands users, permissions, and billing. For teams weighing this tradeoff, reviewing SaaS UX design best practices early, before the architecture is locked in, is one of the cheaper ways to avoid redesigning core screens after launch.
Common mistakes that quietly delay an MVP launch
Most MVP delays do not come from one dramatic event. They come from a handful of avoidable habits that each add a few days, until the launch date has moved without anyone deciding to move it.

rows: Scope keeps expanding mid-build because nothing was deliberately cut
Problems a few days of testing would catch get discovered in production instead
Designing every screen before building any of them
Feedback from the build surfaces design issues too late to fix cheaply
Running feedback rounds in parallel, not in sequence
Conflicting notes from different stakeholders send the same screen back more than once
Adding integrations after the architecture is set
Retrofitting a dependency usually costs more time than planning for it from the start
Confusing flows ship, and the fixes happen in public instead of in design

body.html: None of these mistakes are unusual, and none of them require a bigger budget to avoid. What they require is deciding, before kickoff, what is actually in scope and what every stakeholder's role is in reviewing the work. Teams that are still working out what a UI/UX design engagement should include often find that research, testing, and handoff, not just screens, are exactly the line items that protect a timeline too.
A short decision guide: is your MVP actually ready to scope?
Before asking anyone for a launch date, it helps to check your own answers to a few questions first.

items: You can describe the core user flow in two or three sentences, without an "and also."
You know which user roles exist at launch, and which ones can wait for version two.
You have listed every third-party system the product depends on, not just the obvious ones.
You know who signs off on design decisions and how quickly they typically respond.
You have decided, on purpose, what is explicitly out of scope for version one.

body.html: The more of these you can answer before the first design file opens, the more reliable your timeline will be. Not because the work itself gets faster, but because fewer decisions get made mid-build, and mid-build decisions are where most timelines quietly slip.
The takeaway

There is no universal number that answers "how long does MVP development take," because the real answer depends on what you are actually building, not on what the label promises. A tightly scoped, single-platform product moves fast. A multi-role product with integrations and a review process moves slower, no matter which team builds it. What you can control is scope clarity, how many systems you depend on, and how fast your team turns feedback around, and all three of those are decided well before a single screen gets designed.
Planning an MVP and want a realistic timeline instead of a guess? Tell us what you are building and we will walk you through what it actually takes to get it live.

faq.q: How long does it take to build an MVP?
faq.a: It depends mainly on scope and complexity rather than a fixed timeline. A single-platform product with one clear user flow typically moves faster than a multi-role SaaS product with integrations and a compliance review, since each addition multiplies the screens and states that need to be built and tested.

faq.q: What takes the longest in MVP development?
faq.a: Build and integration is usually the longest phase, because every screen state sketched in design has to actually work in software, including edge cases that only surface once real code is written. Design is often the second longest, especially when the core flow needs several rounds of testing to get right.

faq.q: Does adding more features slow down an MVP?
faq.a: Yes, usually by more than expected. Each added feature, user role, or integration does not simply add its own time. It also adds new interactions with everything already in scope, which is why a tightly defined list of must-have features is one of the most effective ways to protect a launch date.

faq.q: Can an MVP launch faster with a bigger team?
faq.a: Only to a point. Adding people helps with parallel work, but it does not fix an unclear scope or shorten a third-party review cycle, which are often the actual source of a delay. A clearer brief usually moves the date more than extra headcount.

faq.q: What is the biggest cause of MVP delays?
faq.a: Unclear scope at kickoff. When the core flow and the must-have features are not written down and agreed on before design starts, decisions that should have happened on day one get made mid-build instead, which is where most timelines quietly slip.

posts.title: What Does Custom Web Development Actually Cost?
posts.excerpt: Custom web development cost depends on backend complexity, not page count. Here's what drives the number and how to compare quotes fairly.
takeaways: Custom web development cost is driven mainly by backend complexity, not page count: data modeling, custom auth, integrations, QA depth, and post-launch maintenance.
Low-code, hybrid, and fully custom are three different approaches, and the right one depends on how much of the product is truly unique rather than how big it feels.
Fixed-scope pricing suits settled requirements. An ongoing retainer suits a product that keeps evolving.
Compare development quotes by what they include, not by the total alone: architecture, integrations, QA, and maintenance should each be visible.

body.html: What does custom web development actually cost?

Custom web development cost varies by scope, backend complexity, and how many systems the site needs to talk to, not by a fixed price per page. A marketing site with a contact form and a logged-in product with custom permissions, a database of its own, and three external integrations will carry very different price tags even if both get called "a website." The number you should expect depends less on how many pages you want and more on what has to be built behind those pages: data models, authentication, integrations, and the testing that keeps all of it working.
That is the short answer. The rest of this guide breaks down exactly what moves the number, how build approaches change it, and what questions expose a quote that is missing something.
The short answer, in one paragraph

Design cost and development cost are often quoted together, but they are driven by different things. Design cost scales with screens and flows. Development cost scales with what sits behind those screens: how complex the data model is, how much custom logic the backend needs, how many third-party systems get connected, how deep the testing has to go, and what happens after launch. A site that looks simple on the front end can still carry a heavy backend, and that is where most underestimated quotes go wrong.
What actually drives custom development cost
1. Data modeling and backend architecture

Every custom site or app is built on a data model: the entities it tracks (users, orders, listings, bookings) and how they relate to each other. A simple model with one or two entities is quick to build and quick to test. A model with several roles, nested relationships, and state that changes over time (an order that moves through statuses, a booking that can be rescheduled) takes longer to design correctly and longer to get right the first time. Getting the data model wrong early is one of the most expensive mistakes in a build, because fixing it later usually means touching the backend, the frontend, and the database all at once.
2. Custom authentication and permissions

Logging in with an email and password is a solved problem. Logging in with multiple user roles, each seeing a different set of data and a different set of actions, is not. Custom auth with role-based permissions, team accounts, or single sign-on adds real engineering time, both to build and to test, because every role needs to be checked against every protected action. This is one of the factors that most often gets left out of a rough estimate and shows up later as a change request.
3. Integrations with other systems

Payments, CRM, email platforms, shipping carriers, internal tools, analytics: every system your site needs to talk to adds setup time, error handling, and a new thing that can break. A single clean integration with good documentation is a day or two of work. An integration with a flaky API, no sandbox environment, or inconsistent data takes much longer, and you often cannot tell which kind you are dealing with until the build is underway. This is why integration-heavy projects are harder to quote with confidence upfront.
4. Custom UI versus assembled components

A dashboard with standard tables, forms, and charts can be built faster using well-tested patterns. A fully custom interaction, like a drag-and-drop builder, a real-time collaborative view, or a highly specific data visualization, takes meaningfully longer, because there is no existing pattern to lean on. It is worth asking, screen by screen, which parts of the interface are standard and which are truly custom, because the custom ones carry most of the frontend cost.
5. QA and testing depth

Testing scales with what there is to break. A static site needs a pass for broken links and responsive layout. A product with user roles, payments, and integrations needs functional testing across every role, edge-case testing for what happens when an integration fails, and often security testing around anything that touches user data. Testing is the phase most likely to get compressed under a deadline, and it is also the phase where that compression shows up fastest in the first weeks after launch.
6. Maintenance and what happens after launch

A custom build does not stop costing money at launch. Dependencies need updating, integrations can change their APIs without warning, and real users find edge cases nobody anticipated. Budgeting only for the build and not for the months after it is one of the most common ways a project ends up feeling more expensive than it was quoted to be.
Quick reference: what drives cost, low vs high impact

Several systems, flaky APIs, no sandbox

body.html: How do you decide between custom, low-code, and hybrid?

Not every project needs a fully custom build, and conflating the two is a common way budgets get set wrong in both directions. A low-code or no-code platform can get a standard flow (a booking form, a simple marketplace, a content site) live quickly and cheaply, because the platform has already solved the common cases. The tradeoff shows up the moment your requirements step outside what the platform expects: custom logic, a non-standard data model, or an integration the platform does not support natively. At that point, work that would have been simple in a custom build becomes a workaround, and workarounds tend to be fragile.

A hybrid approach, a custom backend for the part of the product that is truly different, with no-code or lighter tooling for the rest, is often the most cost-efficient path for products that have one complex core (a matching algorithm, a pricing engine, a scheduling system) surrounded by standard flows (account pages, settings, contact forms). It takes more planning upfront to decide where the seam between custom and no-code sits, but it keeps cost proportional to actual complexity instead of paying custom rates for every screen.

A fully custom build makes sense once the product has enough custom logic, enough integrations, or enough scale that a platform's limits would start working against you. It costs more upfront and gives you full control over the data model, the auth system, and how everything scales, which tends to pay off as the product grows rather than at launch.
Fixed scope vs ongoing retainer: which pricing model fits?

Development projects are usually priced one of two ways. A fixed-scope project works when requirements are settled: a defined site, a defined MVP, a clear list of features. You know the number before work starts, and changes to scope go through a change request. An ongoing retainer works when the product keeps evolving: a growing platform adding features every sprint, a backend that needs continuous integration work as new systems get added. You are paying for capacity over time rather than a single deliverable.

Picking the wrong model creates friction either way. A fixed-scope project with a roadmap that keeps shifting turns into a stream of change requests that erodes the certainty you paid for. A retainer on a settled, well-defined scope can feel open-ended when a fixed number would have given you more clarity. If you are unsure which fits, write down whether your requirements are likely to change in the next few months. If the honest answer is yes, a retainer usually fits better.
Common mistakes that inflate the real cost

items: Treating the data model as an afterthought. Rushing straight to screens without mapping out entities and relationships leads to rework once real use cases surface gaps in the model.
Skipping a technical discovery phase. A short discovery phase that maps integrations, data, and edge cases upfront is far cheaper than discovering them mid-build.
Under-scoping QA. Treating testing as a buffer at the end of a timeline instead of a planned phase is one of the most common ways launch dates slip.
Choosing a platform before the requirements are clear. Picking a low-code tool because it is familiar, then hitting its limits halfway through, often costs more than starting with the right approach.
No plan for maintenance. Budgeting only for launch and not for the months after it leaves no room for the inevitable fixes and dependency updates.
Comparing quotes by total only. Two quotes with the same number can cover very different scopes. One without research, testing, or a maintenance plan is not cheaper, it is incomplete.

body.html: A short decision guide before you request a quote

items: List every entity your product needs to track and how they relate to each other. If you cannot do this in a page, the project is more complex than it looks.
Count the external systems you need to connect to, and note which ones you have tested access to already.
Decide which parts of the product are truly custom and which are standard flows a platform could handle.
Be honest about whether your requirements will change over the next few months, which should guide fixed-scope versus retainer.
Ask what happens after launch: who fixes what breaks, and what that costs on an ongoing basis.

body.html: If you are earlier in the process and still deciding whether to build custom at all, our guide on custom development versus no-code walks through that decision in more depth. If design and development costs are both on your mind, see what we cover in how much UI/UX design costs. And if you are comparing studios rather than approaches, our breakdown of what a design agency actually costs is a useful companion to this one.
How to compare development quotes fairly
Two quotes with the same total can represent very different projects. Before comparing numbers, check what each quote actually includes.

If one quote lists integrations by name and testing as a separate line, and another gives you a single number with no breakdown, you are not comparing the same project, even if the totals look close. A guide like our website redesign checklist is useful here too, since many of the same scoping questions apply whether you are starting fresh or rebuilding.
What should you expect to provide as a client?
Cost is not only a function of what a development team builds, it is also shaped by how smoothly the project runs, and that depends partly on you.

items: Clear requirements. A written list of what the product needs to do, even in plain language, saves a round of back-and-forth before architecture work can start.
Access to systems early. If an integration needs API keys, sandbox access, or a contact at another vendor, sort that out before the build reaches that integration, not during it.
One point of contact for decisions. Conflicting feedback from multiple stakeholders is one of the most common sources of delay, and delay on a retainer or hourly model has a direct cost.
Realistic content and data. Real sample data, not placeholder text, surfaces edge cases in the data model earlier, when they are cheap to fix.

body.html: The takeaway

Custom web development cost is not really about how many pages a site has. It is about what sits behind those pages: how complex the data is, how much custom logic the backend carries, how many systems it has to talk to, how deep the testing needs to go, and what it takes to keep it running after launch. A fully custom build, a hybrid approach, or a low-code platform can all be the right answer, and the right one depends on how much of what you are building is truly unique. If you can describe your data model, your integrations, and what happens after launch, you can get a quote that reflects the actual project rather than a guess.
Scoping a build and want a number tied to your actual requirements instead of a range? Tell us what you're building and we'll walk through what it would take.

faq.q: What is the biggest factor in custom web development cost?
faq.a: Backend complexity drives the number more than anything else: how many entities the data model tracks, how custom the authentication and permissions are, and how many outside systems the site needs to integrate with.

faq.q: Is custom development more expensive than using a website builder?
faq.a: It costs more upfront because there is no existing platform doing part of the work for you. For products with custom logic or heavy integrations, that upfront cost often pays off through fewer platform limits and lower rework later.

faq.q: Should I choose a fixed price or a retainer for a development project?
faq.a: A fixed price fits a settled, well-defined scope. A retainer fits a product that keeps adding features or changing direction, since you are paying for ongoing capacity rather than a single deliverable.

faq.q: What do cheap development quotes usually leave out?
faq.a: Data modeling and architecture time, a dedicated QA phase, and a plan for post-launch maintenance are the most common gaps in a quote that looks cheaper than it actually is.

faq.q: How long does a custom web development project take?
faq.a: It depends on the data model, the number of integrations, and how custom the interface is. A simple custom build can take a few weeks. A product with multiple roles and integrations takes longer.

body.html: Why is choosing a web design agency harder than it looks?

Most agency websites look impressive. Polished case studies, big client logos, smooth animations. The problem is that a portfolio shows you the finished result, not how the team got there, how long it took, or whether the client was happy with the process.

That gap matters because a website project is months of shared work. You will review designs, answer questions, write or approve content, and live with the platform choice for years. If the fit is wrong, you feel it in missed deadlines, surprise costs, and a site your team cannot update.
The short answer

Choose a web design agency that understands your business goal, explains its process in plain words, tells you exactly who will do the work, recommends a platform for a reason, and has a clear plan for after launch. Ask the 12 questions below on your first calls, and compare the answers side by side.
What are the 12 questions to ask a web design agency?
We grouped the questions into four themes. You do not need to ask all of them in one call. Use the first call for fit and process, and the second for build and support.
Fit: is this the right team for you?

A good agency can describe its ideal client in one or two sentences. If the answer is "everyone", the team probably does not have a clear point of view. Look for experience with your type of business, your stage, or your kind of website, such as a SaaS marketing site, a service business, or a content-heavy blog.

Ask them to explain one case study in detail: the goal, what they changed, what went wrong, and the result. Real teams talk about trade-offs and problems. A pitch that only mentions wins is a script, not experience.

The answer tells you whether design starts from strategy or from taste. Strong teams ask about your audience, your offer, your competitors, and what the website should make people do. If they jump straight to colors and fonts, expect a pretty site that does not move your numbers.
Process: how will the work actually happen?

Kickoff shows how organized a team is. You should hear about a discovery session, a content and sitemap plan, and a clear list of what they need from you, such as access to analytics, brand files, and a decision maker.

At larger agencies, the people on the sales call are often not the people doing the work. Ask for names and roles. Ask whether any part of the design or development is outsourced to freelancers or another company. There is nothing wrong with partners, but you should know who they are.
Most budget arguments come from unclear revision rules. A clear answer sounds like: two rounds on the homepage design, one round on inner pages, and anything beyond that is quoted before work starts.
Build: what are you actually getting?

The platform should follow your needs, not the agency's habits. A marketing team that edits pages every week has different needs from a store with thousands of products. If you are weighing options, our Webflow vs WordPress comparison and Webflow vs Framer guide explain the trade-offs.

These should be part of the build, not an extra you remember at launch. Ask how they keep existing URLs and rankings, how they check page speed, and which accessibility standard they design to. A redesign that drops your search traffic is an expensive mistake. Our website redesign checklist covers what should happen here.

You should own everything you pay for: the Figma files, the site, the hosting account, the domain, and the analytics. Get this in writing. Some agencies host sites on their own accounts, which makes it hard to leave later.
After launch: what happens when you go live?
Listen for a checklist: redirects, forms, tracking, mobile checks on real devices, and a rollback plan. A calm launch is the result of preparation, not luck.
Your marketing team should be able to publish a blog post or change a headline without opening a support ticket. Ask whether training, documentation, or a short video walkthrough is included.

Sites need fixes, updates, and new pages. Ask about response times, what a support plan costs, and whether the same team stays involved. The most common complaint after launch is slow responses, so settle this before you sign.
How do you go from a long list to a signed contract?

The questions work best inside a simple process. Each stage should end with something you can check, such as a one-page brief, a shortlist, or a written scope. If a stage has no output, it is easy to skip and hard to defend later.
What red flags and green flags should you watch for?
Some warning signs appear in the very first conversation. Others show up in the proposal. Here are the patterns we see most often when clients come to us after a project went wrong.
Red flags

items: Guaranteed rankings or results. Nobody controls Google or your market. Promises like "page one in 30 days" are sales lines.
The same package for every client. If the proposal could be sent to any business, it was not written for yours.
No questions about your goals. A team that does not ask about your customers is designing for itself.
Vague ownership or hosting terms. If you cannot leave with your site and files, you are renting, not buying.
A price with no scope attached. A single number without pages, rounds, and deliverables will grow later.

body.html: Green flags

items: They ask about your business before talking about design.
They explain their process in plain words and show real examples of it.
The proposal lists pages, deliverables, timeline, and who does what.
They tell you when something is not a good idea, even if it means less work for them.
They have a clear plan for training and support after launch.

body.html: How do you compare web design proposals fairly?

Proposals rarely line up neatly. One agency quotes a low number with fewer pages, another includes copywriting and SEO, a third bundles a year of support. To compare them, put the proposals in a simple table with the same rows for each agency. Here is the layout we suggest.

rows: Number and type of pages, plus blog and CMS templates
Extra pages are the most common source of added cost
Skipping it leads to redesigns later
Rounds included and how extra changes are priced
Who owns the accounts and pays for hosting
Ownership decides whether you can leave
Migration, testing, and standards named in writing
Who writes it and who loads it
Content delays are the top cause of late launches
Dates, including the ones you are responsible for
Projects slip when client tasks are vague
What is included after launch and response times
Your team needs to run the site without help

body.html: Once the scope is visible, the price differences usually make sense. If you want a deeper look at what moves the number, read how much a SaaS website costs and how UI/UX design is priced.
How do you score the agencies you shortlist?

After the calls, score each agency on the same criteria. A simple one to five scale is enough. The point is to make the gaps visible, so the conversation with your team is about evidence, not gut feeling.
Should you hire a freelancer, a small studio, or a large agency?

There is no single right size. A freelancer can be a great fit for a small, well-defined site with a tight budget, but you depend on one person's time and skills. A large agency brings many specialists and process, but you may pay for layers of management and see less of the senior team. A small, senior studio sits in between.

rows: Direct contact, flexible, good for small defined sites
One person's capacity, and gaps outside their skill
Design and development together, fewer handoffs
Check availability and how support works
Layers of management, junior staff doing the work

body.html: A small studio gives you design and development under one roof, direct contact with the people doing the work, and fewer handoffs. That is the model we run at The Shark Web, because we have seen how much quality is lost when strategy, design, and development are split across different companies.
What are the most common mistakes when hiring an agency?

items: Choosing on price alone. A low quote with a thin scope often costs more once changes start.
Judging only by the portfolio. Looks do not show process, communication, or results.
Skipping the brief. Without a clear goal, every proposal answers a different question.
Talking to only one agency. You cannot judge a proposal without something to compare it against.
Not asking who does the work. The team you meet may not be the team you get.
Ignoring ownership terms. Discovering at the end that you do not own the site is a costly surprise.
Forgetting your own tasks. Content, feedback, and approvals from your side decide the timeline as much as the agency does.

body.html: What is a simple process for choosing?

items: Write one sentence that describes what the new website must achieve.
Shortlist three to five agencies whose work and clients match your needs.
Run a 30-minute call with each and ask the fit and process questions.
Request proposals from your top two or three, with the same brief for each.
Compare scope, process, and ownership in a table, then compare price.
Speak to one past client of your preferred agency before you sign.

body.html: A checklist before you sign

items: The proposal lists pages, deliverables, rounds of feedback, and timeline.
You know who will design and build the site, and who your contact is.
The platform choice comes with a reason that fits your team.
SEO migration, speed, and accessibility are named in the scope.
Ownership of files, code, domain, hosting, and analytics is in writing.
Training and support after launch are included or priced.
You have spoken to at least one past client.

body.html: The takeaway

The right agency is the one that understands your goal, is clear about how it works, and tells you the truth before you sign. If you are planning a new site or a redesign, talk to The Shark Web team. We will answer every question on this list, including the uncomfortable ones.

articles.body:
The client buys shops, and every shop comes with a website

The client is a retail group with a large number of locations. Part of what they sell is bought in the shop. Part is a service delivered on site, by appointment. The catalogue splits into two segments, a luxury one and an everyday one.

They grow by acquisition. They buy small independent retailers and bring them into the group. Some keep their own brand, some are moved onto the group’s. It depends on how the deal was made.

Every acquisition arrives with one or more websites. These sites usually have traffic and may or may not have a product catalogue on it. Sites run on whatever the previous owner’s agency preferred at the time.

So this is not an estate that accumulated once and then sat still. The business produces new websites as a side effect of doing business. Everything below follows from that.

What a few days of reading found

We were asked to take five sites into maintenance. All from the luxury segment, all on WordPress, all running roughly the same engine.

We spent a few days on what was there and told them what we found:

  • old WordPress
  • a zoo of plugins, different versions on every site
  • themes built in Elementor, which looks fine in the browser and is painful to maintain
  • products entered separately on every site, filled in the same way in some places and at random in others

The budget was small, so the plan we gave them was small as well. Maintenance, upgrades, and getting the zoo into some order. On WordPress. We were not proposing to replace anything at that point.

First: make them the same

We updated WordPress and the plugins everywhere and unified as much as we could.

That made the sites safer to touch. It did not make it possible to change anything across all of them at once.

Second: the tools that manage many WordPress sites

Next we looked at central management. One place, many sites, one database behind them.

We tried practically everything on the market, ten or fifteen tools. Some we took on trial, some we installed self-hosted to see how far they went. They differ in where they run and who they are built for, more technical or more for managers. Underneath that they are much the same.

None of them solved the thing that actually mattered. Sites are still hard to support. Products were still not managed centrally.

Third: the CSV detour

So we built it ourselves. Export products from each site to CSV. Generate new CSV files with the new products, half by script and half by hand. Import them back into each site through WP-CLI. We also used custom script + WP-CLI to update sites’ core and plugins.

On paper this is workable. In practice it was bad:

  • only a developer could run any of it
  • there was no real control over who published what, or where
  • we spent a lot of time on it and most of that time was wasted

I would rather write that we went from the audit to the right answer. We did not. We spent weeks finding out that the problem was not going to be solved from inside WordPress.

What the actual problem was

Two things, and neither of them is about code quality.

Products could not be managed centrally, and that got worse with every site added. And a site on WordPress was slow to build. Not expensive, slow. A month, often several.

For a business that adds a site every time it buys a shop, that is the whole problem.

The proposal

One place for the data, many frontends.

Strapi holds products, content and everything else, centrally. Next to it, one frontend per site, generated to static. Astro for the frontends, which we had been using heavily by then and which had behaved well every time.

The client approved the scope and the budget and we started.

The dull decision that made it affordable

The first migration had no redesign in it. We ported the templates one to one, and we deliberately dragged old libraries along with them.

The markup on most pages stayed as it was. Everything under it was new.

This is the decision I would defend hardest. Rebuilding the front end at the same time as the back end would have doubled the cost of proving that the idea worked, and the client had not signed up to find out twice.

Components came afterwards, pulled out of five sites that were already running. Not designed up front.

One library, then clones

We took the repeating pieces and turned them into reusable components, each with its own settings, so a site could be assembled from parts instead of built.

The sites are multilingual, so that was built into the components rather than added to them later. A component that cannot hold a second language is a component you rewrite.

After that, most of the work on a new site is styles that override defaults which are already tested and already working.

And don’t forget that we had always tried to expose colors/images and other style related thiongs into component’s properties that inherited site’s visual settings.

At that point we had five sites that shared one product database, could each be customised down to which products appeared on them, and updated quickly.

Plugins, because Strapi manages content and not an estate

Strapi out of the box is a CMS. An estate needs more than that, so the useful work went into plugins.

Sites builder. Building from the command line was fine for us and no use to anyone else. The builder watches Strapi for changes, collects them, triggers the Astro rebuilds, and reports what changed, where and when.

Brands and products overview. Per site and per brand, where every product is currently shown, with checkboxes to turn products on and off. Worth saying here that these sites are catalogues. There is no checkout on them.

Shopify synchroniser. More on that below.

Import and export. This one exists because the client kept arriving with spreadsheets of new stock that was not in Shopify and not anywhere else, asking us to get it onto all of the sites.

The transactional side

In parallel, and separately, the group runs its actual selling on Shopify Plus. We worked on that too: custom apps for inventory and ERP synchronisation, and a custom checkout. That side was mostly backend work, done as outstaff, with several of our people embedded in the client’s team.

Once both sides were healthy, we connected them. Products sync from Shopify into Strapi, which gives the group one place where images, descriptions and the rest live in the same shape.

What came in through the door

Not everything arriving was WordPress. Wix, Squarespace. Plain static HTML. Other CMSs. Some of them nobody could name.

A few sites had no admin access left at all. The company had bought the business, and the credentials were gone. The only copy of the site we had was the one the public could see, so that is what we rebuilt from.

Four instances, for a reason that is not technical

The sites do not all run on one instance. There are four.

The reason is organisational. This is a large enterprise, and inside it departments compete with each other and do not always overlap. Same infrastructure, separate instances, and everyone keeps their own.

The same stack also carries sites that have nothing to do with products. The corporate site. Sites whose whole job is booking an appointment. That last one leans on an integration with the group’s booking system, which exposes specialist availability per location through an API, and having one engine meant we could put it wherever it was wanted.

Where it is now

Development started in 2023. The numbers today:

  • 50+ sites on the stack, across four instances
  • a new site takes up to a week, and most of that week is implementation of design
  • before, on WordPress, a site took a month, sometimes several
  • the team went from one person at the start to four or five at the busiest point
  • in good months we added three to five sites, with pauses of a month or two to refactor what had accumulated

The part I would point at first: when a new site resembles one we have already built, the client’s own managers do it. We clone an existing site for them, and they change the colour scheme, load the images and handle the rest. No developer in the loop.

They run the content and the sites themselves now. Adding a site still needs us for a few things, and removing that is the next piece of work.

There is no clean sweep to report. Some sites are still on their old platforms and will move when there is a reason to move them. That work is ongoing, the same way the acquisitions are.

If your estate looks like this

Four things worth checking, in this order.

  1. Name the thing that cannot be managed centrally. If it is content, tools for that already exist and you should buy one. If it is product data, they will not help you, and we lost months confirming it.
  2. Do not redesign during a migration. Move the thing first, with its old markup if that is what makes it cheap. You are proving the architecture, not the visuals.
  3. Extract components after, not before. A component library designed up front is a guess. One pulled out of five working sites is a record of what actually repeats.
  4. The test is whether a non-developer can add a site. As long as the answer is no, you have moved the bottleneck rather than removed it.

If you are looking at an estate like this and are not sure whether it is a consolidation or fifty separate projects, that is a question worth answering before anyone writes code.
